rooms.question: Does a graph already contain the order in which we should visit it?
rooms.ontology: A graph separates vertices from their connections. A traversal adds an order ofvisiting to that relation.
rooms.action: Choose one of the15lamps. Watch the blue tide and then the amber diver reach it; predict which neighbouringlamp lights next.
rooms.observable: The tide lights successivelevels; the diver follows a branch before returning to another. The same lamps and edges remainthroughout.
rooms.mechanism: Both orders are actually computed from one adjacencylist: BFS removes from aqueuefront, DFS removes from a stackback. The orders replay at.45seconds pervisit with a pausebetween.
rooms.limit: A drawnheight is not inherent importance, and traversalorder is not the graph itself. A tree also lacks the cycleambiguities of generalgraphs.
rooms.variation: Existing: follow a deep lamp rather than the root, making its delay the comparison. Proposed: let thevisitor choose the startingvertex or add a cycle.
rooms.prior_bridge: Machinelearning classified samples; graphs begin by asking what connections we retain.
rooms.next_bridge: The next room moves the drawing while retaining theconnections.
cautions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.

rooms.question: Can the picture change while the graph stays the same?
rooms.ontology: A layout assigns spatialpositions to vertices. Adjacency says whichvertices are joined and can remain unchanged throughout that movement.
rooms.action: Track one movingvertex and count its links before and after the drawing settles.
rooms.observable: Eightvertices move while the same12connections stretch and turn; the defaultgraph is the cubegraph drawn in aplane.
rooms.mechanism: Connectedpairs attract through springs; allpairs repel. Dampedvelocity integrates forces, so initialpositions influence the eventualdrawing.
rooms.limit: Closeness on the page is a layoutresult, not necessarily a directconnection. A neatdrawing does not prove its arrangement uniquely represents the graph.
rooms.variation: Existing: compare what you thought was central before/afterrelaxation. Proposed: expose alternate initialpositions with fixedadjacency, then try a ring or star as anexplicit differentgraph.
rooms.prior_bridge: The same tree supported two itineraries; now the same adjacency supports changingpositions.
rooms.next_bridge: Pathfinding will change connections rather than merelymoving their picture.
cautions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.

rooms.question: What happens to the shortest route when a stone disappears?
rooms.ontology: A route is a sequence ofconnected vertices. Shortest refers to summed edgecost on the currentgraph, not the traveller remembering a line.
rooms.action: Follow the spark between riverbanks, press thebutton to sink a stone, and compare the next computedroute. Repeat to see an oldstone return after the queue exceeds3.
rooms.observable: A route stone lowers and becomes unavailable; the spark is replanned immediately. Some removals can yield a NO ROUTE message instead of a detour.
rooms.mechanism: AStar3D connects nearby stones within1.05units, with extra bankconnections. The button disables a routepoint and keeps at most3disabled stones; each bankarrival also recomputes thepath.
rooms.limit: The spark queries agraph, not actualhuman jumpingability. A drawn stone is not a verified walkablesurface or a promise that every removal has analternatepath.
rooms.variation: Existing: intentionally interrupt the route and treat waiting or disconnection as an outcome. Proposed: permit a slower accessible route objective alongside Euclideandistance.
rooms.prior_bridge: Moving a graphpicture left adjacency intact; sinking a stone changes which routes exist.
rooms.next_bridge: Networkanalysis asks what eachconnection contributes to thewhole.
cautions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.

rooms.question: Is the biggest node the one whose connections matter most?
rooms.ontology: Degree counts immediateconnections; othercentrality measures answer different questions about routes or influence. Drawing a hub is distinct from measuring one.
rooms.action: Choose one largenode and one smallnode. Count their visibleconnections and trace at least one route through each before trusting its visualrank.
rooms.observable: The scene stages5central,8middle and12peripheral nodes, connecting and animating them with deliberately different sizes andcolours.
rooms.mechanism: Tierlabels and centralityvalues are assigned when nodes arecreated. The displayed clustering/connectivity variables vary with time, not computed graphstatistics.
rooms.limit: This is a networkdiagram, not a validatedcentrality calculator. Sizeandcolour may guide a hypothesis but cannot serve as evidence that its assignedtier isimportant.
rooms.variation: Existing: begin from a peripheralnode and identify what its routespermit. Proposed: compute and show actual degree orbetweenness, then compare with the originalvisual hierarchy.
rooms.prior_bridge: The river showed that removing a node can change routes; now ask which relationships would be lost.
rooms.next_bridge: Directedconnectivity next requires that a route can alsocomeback.
cautions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.
Central concept gap: calculatecentrality from adjacency before treating visualhierarchy asalgorithmic result.

rooms.question: If you can reach another node, can you get back?
rooms.ontology: A strongly connectedcomponent is a maximal set whosevertices can reach eachother along directedpaths. One-way contact is insufficient.
rooms.action: Pick two vertices joined by anarrow, then trace a returnroute. Watch the automaticsearch assign componentcolours and compare its grouping with your prediction.
rooms.observable: Current, visited, backedge andcomponent colours expose a depth-firstsearch; the status announces each discoveredcomponent.
rooms.mechanism: Tarjan records discoverytimes and lowlinks, keeps activevertices on astack, and pops a component when a completedvertex has lowlink equal to its discoverytime.
rooms.limit: Mutualreachability is a precise relation in this directedgraph, not mutualtrust, equality or universalaccess. A one-way bridge can connect a drawing without merging its strongcomponents.
rooms.variation: Existing: search for a route that leaves acomponent and cannot return. Proposed: expose a reversiblearrow and observe whichcomponents merge.
rooms.prior_bridge: Visualnetworkrank depended on representation; directedreachability gives an explicit groupingrule.
rooms.next_bridge: Spanningtrees ask how few connections can retain reachability in anundirected graph.
cautions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.

rooms.question: Which connections can be removed while keeping everyone connected?
rooms.ontology: A spanningtree connects everyvertex withoutcycles. A minimumspanningtree minimizes totaledgeweight among suchtrees for a connectedweighted undirectedgraph.
rooms.action: Watch candidateedges receive attention and greenedges join thebackbone. Before eachdecision, predict whether accepting theedge would close acycle.
rooms.observable: Acceptededges accumulate until the backboneconnects allvertices; some edges are skipped even when short because their ends already belong to thesamecomponent.
rooms.mechanism: The defaultKruskal path sorts byweight and uses union-find to reject cycleclosingedges. Weight is assigned from the generatedgraph; the nextlowest eligibleedge joins components.
rooms.limit: Lowesttotalcost does not provide redundantconnections. Every treeedge is a singlepoint of disconnection if removed; reliability may justify an extraedge.
rooms.variation: Existing: mentally remove an acceptededge and identify the two resultinggroups. Proposed: compare the cheapesttree with a deliberately redundantnetwork and name the extracost.
rooms.prior_bridge: Strongcomponents asked about roundtrips; now connectivity must survive deliberateedge removal.
rooms.next_bridge: Flowadds capacity and asks how much can pass through connections.
cautions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.

rooms.question: When a junction receives more than it can send onward, where does the excess go?
rooms.ontology: Capacity limits anedge; flow is the currentallocation; excess is netmaterial held temporarily at anintermediatevertex. Height is analgorithmiclabel used to routeupdates.
rooms.action: Follow the sourceoutflow, then watch a junction with excess and read its PUSH orRELABEL status.
rooms.observable: Sourceedges fill first; a vertex may pass availableflow to a lowerheight neighbour or change itsheight when itcannotpush. Pervertexheight/excess and overallflow labels are drawn.
rooms.mechanism: The implementation initializes apreflow, then pushes min(excess,residualcapacity) on originaloutgoingedges whose height islower. Relabelling examines availableoutgoing capacity.
rooms.limit: A full maximumflow solver needs residualreverse edges so earlierallocations can be undone. This implementation does not maintain them and cannot support its blanket maximumclaim.
rooms.variation: Proposed nextbuild: draw reversible residualcapacity and let visitors inspect a rerouting case; meanwhile compare a localpush to the sinktotal without assuming everylocaldecision isfinal.
rooms.prior_bridge: A tree retained connectivity; capacity introduces bottlenecks even where pathsremain.
rooms.next_bridge: Matching next limits eachvertex to one selectedpartner.

sources.fact: Onlyoriginal outgoingedges updated; residualreverse state absent.

cautions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.
Centralalgorithm gap: do not assert maximumflow, standardpush-relabel invariants or completion on everygraph. No visitoralgorithm controlsverified.

rooms.question: Can an early pairing prevent a larger set of pairings later?
rooms.ontology: A matching is a set ofedges with no sharedendpoint. A maximalmatching cannot add anotheredge; a maximummatching has the largestpossible number ofedges. These are differentclaims.
rooms.action: Watch the next highlightededge. Predict acceptance by checking whether bothendpoints are still unmatched; track onevertex leftwithout a partner.
rooms.observable: Edgesare scanned in their storedorder. When bothendpoints are free they become a pair, and neither is reconsideredlater.
rooms.mechanism: process_matching_step implements a greedy scan. There is no augmentingpath search or blossomcontraction, despite the artifactname and completioncaption saying maximum.
rooms.limit: A completegreedy scan gives a maximalmatching, not necessarilymaximum. On a fourvertexpath, choosing the middleedge first leavesone pair where choosing bothouteredges would giv two.
rooms.variation: Proposed: expose edgeorder or a4vertexpath counterexample, then add augmentingpath updates. Existing: identify which earlierpair blocks a latercandidate.
rooms.prior_bridge: Flowallocated capacities; matching makes a discrete onepartnerconstraint visible.
rooms.next_bridge: Foundationscrisis asks what a formalprocedure can and cannot establish from its ownrules.
cautions: Source-reviewed draft; current museum reach, readable labels, controls and human learning unverified.
Centralalgorithm gap: this is not Edmonds blossomalgorithm. Preserve teachingintent inrepairqueue; do not presentgreedy as correctmaximumsolver.
